title: Learning to Read UX Flows
body: Learning UX refers to the screen flow and feedback structure designed to help users continue their learning.
detail: UX code for learning isn’t just about creating visually appealing screens; it’s about creating a flow that lets users know what they’ve learned, what they got wrong, and what they need to do next. Features like “progress,” “review,” “mistake note,” “bookmark,” and “streak” all display the user’s learning status or encourage review. When reading the code, consider state management, display conditions, and the user’s next action together.
examples: Collect the questions you got wrong in a "mistake note" so you can review them later.
The "progress" value shows the number of cards solved today and the number of cards remaining.

title: Understanding the Checkpoint and Resume Workflow
body: A checkpoint should record completed IDs, input version, output location, and validation state. File existence alone can mistake a partial output for success, so use atomic writes or a completion marker. On resume, verify duplicates, omissions, and changed inputs.
examples: If the process fails after processing 60 out of 100, it restarts from the 61st.
If an output file already exists, the same items are not processed again.

title: Understanding the GPU·Torch·Training Workflow
body: The model and tensors must use the same device. Training uses loss.backward() and optimizer.step(); inference uses model.eval() to change dropout and batch-normalization behavior and no_grad() or inference_mode() to disable gradient recording. These settings serve different purposes, so check both.
examples: Use `torch.cuda.is_available()` to check whether CUDA is available.
Verify that `model.to(device)` and `tensor.to(device)` point to the same device.

title: Understanding the Security·Settings·Secret Workflow
body: Keep secrets out of code, logs, and clients by injecting them through protected environment or platform secret settings. A local .env is a convenience file, and .gitignore does not protect an already tracked secret. Rotate exposed values and review least privilege, retention, and personal-data transfers.
examples: Read the secret using `os.environ.get('API_KEY')` and do not hardcode it in the code.
Add the .env file to .gitignore so that it isn't pushed to the repository.

title: Understanding the Retry, Timeout, and Resilience Workflow
body: A timeout prevents indefinite waits, while a retry repeats eligible transient failures. Use a maximum, exponential backoff, and jitter. Do not automatically retry a side-effecting request such as POST unless idempotency is guaranteed, and stop immediately for authentication or validation failures.
examples: If a request fails, it will retry up to three times and log the failure.
Set a limit, such as `timeout=10`, to prevent the system from getting stuck waiting for unresponsive requests.

title: Understanding the RAG, Search, and LLM Trends
body: RAG is a method that searches for relevant information and appends it to the LLM's input before answering a question.
detail: The RAG code should be read in the following order: question analysis, query generation, document retrieval, candidate ranking, context construction, and LLM invocation. Since poor search quality can lead to unreliable LLM responses, you must verify what sources were used and why they were selected. Embeddings are used to find documents with similar meanings, while keyword search is advantageous for finding materials that contain exact words.
examples: First, search for any cards or documents related to the question, and then send them to the LLM along with the question.
If there are insufficient search results, it indicates that further verification is needed rather than providing an answer.

title: Understanding FastAPI and Server Workflow
body: The FastAPI code demonstrates a server workflow that receives HTTP requests, processes them using functions, and returns responses.
detail: FastAPI code is easiest to understand when read in the following order: route decorator, path, request parameter, and response model. A line like `@app.get('/items')` maps a specific URL request to the function that will handle it. Since server code receives external input, validation, exception handling, and status codes are also important. During development, run the code using Uvicorn, and in production, be sure to check environment variables and log settings as well.
examples: @app.get('/health') is often used as an API to check the server's status.
Check how the query parameters and JSON body are passed as function arguments.

title: Reading the Input and Output Flow of a Function
body: Function code can be viewed as a small sequence of steps that takes input, processes it, and returns a result.
detail: When reading a function, break it down into its parameters, internal processing, and return value. For functions that involve I/O—such as those handling files, user input, or API responses—you must distinguish between values coming in from the outside and values going out, such as screen output, file saves, and return values. A good function has a single, clear responsibility, and its inputs and outputs are predictable. The easier a function is to test, the easier it is to debug.
examples: def clean_text(text): return text.strip() cleans up the input string and returns it.
It's easier to test the code if you separate the functions that read files from those that calculate data.
